items.title: The U-2 and OXCART Programs
items.summary: Chapter 2 of the CIA's 1992 internal history of its U-2 and OXCART spy-plane programs, from the less-redacted version released in 2013 that names Area 51. It tells how the CIA and Lockheed chose Groom Lake in 1955 and says U-2 and OXCART flights accounted for more than half of all UFO reports in the late 1950s and most of the 1960s.
items.credit: Central Intelligence Agency (Gregory W. Pedlow and Donald E. Welzenbach)

facts.claim: Written by CIA historians Gregory Pedlow and Donald Welzenbach and issued in classified channels in 1992; the less-redacted version came out in answer to a 2005 FOIA request and was posted by the National Security Archive on 15 August 2013.

Every page of this chapter is stamped 'Approved for Release: 2013/06/25'; on 12 April 1955 Bissell, Ritland, Kelly Johnson and Tony LeVier found the old airstrip at Groom Lake, which took the map name Area 51 and which Johnson called the Paradise Ranch.
U-2 and later OXCART flights accounted for more than one-half of all UFO reports during the late 1950s and most of the 1960s.
The CIA reading-room record for document 0000190094 lists 406 pages and a 1992 publication date; this file is Chapter 2, 'Developing the U-2', which starts on page 39.

items.title: CIA Map of Area 51
items.summary: A CIA map from the 1992 U-2 and OXCART history that marks Area 51 and Groom Lake beside the Atomic Energy Commission's Nevada Test Site. It was released in 2013 with the less-redacted history, a release widely reported as the US government's first acknowledgement of the base.

facts.claim: The map page (page 58 of CIA document C00190094) is stamped 'Approved for Release: 2013/06/25' and carries the map code 724741 (R00425) 4-92.

The National Security Archive posted the map as 'The CIA's declassified map of Groom Lake/Area 51' on 15 August 2013 and lists news reports such as 'It's real! US confirms Area 51's existence' and 'Area 51 Finally Acknowledged By US Government'.
The history says the outline of Area 51 is shown on unclassified maps as a small rectangle adjoining the northeast corner of the much larger Nevada Test Site.

items.title: Skylab Photographs Area 51
items.summary: A 1974 memo to CIA Director William Colby reporting that Skylab astronauts had photographed the one place they had been told not to (the name is blacked out; it was Area 51), and that NASA wanted the picture released while Defense Department agencies wanted it withheld. Colby's handwritten note questions the need to protect it, since the Soviets had it from their own satellites, and asks what it really reveals.

facts.claim: CIA memo 'SKYLAB Imagery' dated 19 April 1974 (CIA-RDP80M01048A000800210008-5), 5 pages, stamped 'Approved For Release 2004/10/12'.
The National Security Archive identifies the photographed site as Area 51 and says the memo reports the photo was taken inadvertently despite instructions not to photograph the facility.
The photos were taken by the third and last Skylab crew (Carr, Gibson, Pogue); DoD elements (USAF, NRO, JCS, ISA) wanted the photo withheld while NASA and largely State wanted it released.
Colby's note on the routing slip, dated 4/19/74, questions the need to protect the photo because the USSR has it from its own satellites and asks what it really reveals.

items.title: U-2 in Fake NASA Markings
items.summary: After Francis Gary Powers' CIA U-2 was shot down over the Soviet Union on 1 May 1960, NASA said the plane had been doing weather research. To back the cover story, a U-2 was painted in NASA markings with a made-up serial number and shown to reporters at NASA's Flight Research Center at Edwards on 6 May 1960.

facts.claim: NASA photo E-5442, dated 6 May 1960: a U-2 painted in NASA markings with a fictitious NASA serial number was put on display for the news media at the NASA Flight Research Center, Edwards AFB, on 6 May 1960.
NASA's press release of 5 May 1960 described the missing U-2 as a weather research aircraft (National Archives Identifier 12009392).
The cover story collapsed when the Soviet Union displayed Powers and the wreckage, proving the plane was a reconnaissance aircraft.

items.title: Project HAVE DOUGHNUT
items.summary: The 1969 tactical report on HAVE DOUGHNUT, the 1968 project in which Air Force and Navy pilots secretly flew a Soviet-built MiG-21 at Area 51 against US fighters to learn how to beat it. Israel had lent the jet, which it got when an Iraqi pilot defected with it in 1966.
items.credit: Defense Intelligence Agency (report by the U.S. Air Force Foreign Technology Division)

facts.claim: Report FTD-CR-20-13-69-INT, Vol. II, 'Have Doughnut (U) Tactical', dated 1 August 1969, prepared by the Air Force Foreign Technology Division with TAC, ADC and the Navy for the Defense Intelligence Agency; the cover is stamped 'Declassified IAW E.O. 12958, reviewed by NAIC/TA, 23 Mar 2000'.

Israel obtained the MiG-21 in August 1966 when an Iraqi air force captain defected with it; it was loaned to the US Air Force from 23 January to 8 April 1968 and Area 51 became its home for the HAVE DOUGHNUT exploitation.
The National Security Archive published the 310-page report as Document 50 of 'The Area 51 File: Secret Aircraft and Soviet MiGs' on 29 October 2013.

items.title: A-12 OXCART in Flight
items.summary: An undated 1960s U.S. Air Force photo of the A-12 OXCART, the Mach 3 spy plane Lockheed built for the CIA and test-flew at Area 51 from April 1962. This aircraft, 60-6932, was lost at sea with CIA pilot Jack Weeks in June 1968, shortly before the program ended.

facts.claim: Department of Defense photo DF-SC-82-10542 (Defense Visual Information Center, 1982 catalogue) of A-12 serial 60-6932, undated (1960s); the aircraft was lost in June 1968.
The A-12 made its official first flight from the Nevada site on 30 April 1962, after an unofficial hop on 25 April and a first flight on 26 April, piloted by Louis Schalk.
On 4 June 1968 an A-12 on a test flight from Kadena disappeared 520 miles east of Manila with pilot Jack W. Weeks, just before the planned 8 June phase-out of all OXCART aircraft.

items.title: M-21 Carrying a D-21 Drone
items.summary: An undated U.S. Air Force photo from the 1964-66 test program of M-21 60-6940, a two-seat A-12 rebuilt as a mothership, carrying a D-21 reconnaissance drone on its back. On 30 July 1966 a D-21 struck the other M-21 as it launched, destroying both and killing launch officer Ray Torick; the drone was later launched from B-52s over China instead.

facts.claim: Department of Defense photo DF-SC-82-10541 (dated 6 January 1982 in the DoD catalogue) of M-21 60-6940 carrying a D-21, circa 1964-1966; A-12s 60-6940 and 60-6941 were converted as drone carriers and flight testing began 22 December 1964.
On the fourth M-21/D-21 launch test, 30 July 1966, the drone struck the M-21's tail and destroyed both aircraft; pilot Bill Park survived and the launch control officer drowned.
From November 1969 B-52Hs launched D-21B drones over China in Project Senior Bowl; the last mission, on 20 March 1971, crashed inside China.
The CIA's 2013 history prints a photo captioned 'M-12 carrying D-21 Drone' in its OXCART chapter.

items.title: The SR-71
items.summary: A short U.S. Air Force film of the SR-71 Blackbird, the Air Force's two-seat reconnaissance version of the CIA's A-12, with air-to-air shots, cockpit instruments at about Mach 3 above 80,000 feet, a takeoff and a landing. President Johnson revealed the SR-71 in July 1964; the CIA history says he was meant to say 'RS-71'.
items.credit: U.S. Air Force (Media Production Flight, 367th Training Support Squadron, Hill AFB)

facts.claim: U.S. Air Force film distributed by NTIS as AVA20323 ('The SR-71'); its titles show the USAF 50th-anniversary emblem (1947-1997) and credit the Media Production Flight, 367th Training Support Squadron, Hill AFB, Utah.
On 25 July 1964 President Johnson revealed a new Air Force reconnaissance aircraft he called the SR-71; he was supposed to say RS-71, and the Air Force renamed the aircraft rather than correct him.
In December 1962 the Air Force ordered a longer two-seat reconnaissance version of the OXCART with more sensors, slower and lower-flying than the A-12.

rejected.title: Angels in Paradise: The Development of the U-2 at Area 51 (c. 1960 film)
rejected.reason: The best Area 51 footage (20 min, shot at the base, released by the CIA in 2012; Commons copy 70 MB), but it was made by contractor Hycon Mfg. Co. (Don Downie, Jim Jarboe), so it is not a US government work; Commons tags it PD-USGov with licence review still pending, and the CIA has made its YouTube copy private. Use it only if its licence is cleared.

rejected.title: Throw a Nickel on the Grass: Project HAVE DOUGHNUT (1968 Navy/Air Force film, NARA 271815859)
rejected.reason: Only file is 565 MB (over the 400 MB video cap) and the National Archives catalog marks use as 'Restricted - Possibly' (copyright). Strong video if a transcode under 400 MB is acceptable.

rejected.title: Presidential Determination 95-45 on Groom Lake (Clinton, 1995)
rejected.reason: Not a failure: left out to stay at 8 items. One-page Federal Register PDF verified from govinfo (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1995-10-10/pdf/95-25244.pdf, 200, 301773 bytes) exempting the 'operating location near Groom Lake' from waste-law disclosure amid worker lawsuits; good substitute.

rejected.title: Full CIA history 'The U-2 and OXCART Programs, 1954-1974' (406 pages)
rejected.reason: Over the ~300-page limit (archive.org mirror of CIA document 0000190094 checked: 406 pages). Used Chapter 2 instead, which holds the Area 51 site selection, map and UFO passage.

rejected.title: CORONA satellite image of Area 51
rejected.reason: No specific CORONA frame of Groom Lake could be identified, and USGS EarthExplorer downloads need a login. The 1962 CIA memo proposing CORONA coverage of Area 51 is a one-page item in EBB 443 if wanted.

rejected.title: Skylab photograph of Area 51 (1974)
rejected.reason: The image itself was never released; only the memos about it were. Used the CIA memo instead.

rejected.title: LBJ's 1964 A-11 / SR-71 announcement material (LBJ Library)
rejected.reason: discoverlbj.org returns 403 to scripted downloads; no mirror of the A-11 statement folder or audio found.

rejected.title: A-12 first flight at Groom Lake, 1962 (Commons 'A-12 Schalk Flight, 1962.jpg')
rejected.reason: Provenance unclear: taken from a book promotion site and credited 'CIA/Roadrunners Internationale', also used by Lockheed Martin. Used a DoD-catalogued A-12 photo instead.

rejected.title: CIA Flickr A-12 OXCART photos
rejected.reason: They show the A-12 on display at CIA headquarters in 2011, not historical material.

rejected.title: CIA 'Archangel' monograph images (Kelly Johnson sketches, A-12 pole models, A-12 photo of USS Pueblo at Wonsan)
rejected.reason: Interesting Skunk Works and CIA material, but the copies on Commons are all 800 px or smaller and cia.gov blocks scripted downloads.

rejected.title: The Blackbird Story (1972) on Commons
rejected.reason: The Commons copy is AI-upscaled and 479 MB (over the cap).

rejected.title: U-2 Affair (NBC White Paper, 1962) and Universal Newsreel U-2 reels
rejected.reason: Commercial broadcast and newsreel films, not US government works.

rejected.title: Project HAVE DOUGHNUT - Exploitation of the MiG-21 (Rob Young, NASIC briefing; NSA EBB 443 Document 49)
rejected.reason: Replaced by the 1969 DIA tactical report (Document 50). The briefing is an undated later retrospective by the NASIC historian (it mentions TOP GUN and Red Flag), sourced from a private website, with no verifiable release date.
